title: Event Triggered Execution: AppInit DLLs
summary: The AppInit_DLLs value under the Windows NT key, and its Wow6432Node twin for 32-bit code, tells the user32 library which extra modules to load. Since user32 is loaded by almost every graphical program, an entry there reaches an extremely large number of processes and gives the adversary persistence and a route into processes that hold higher rights. A companion value, LoadAppInit_DLLs, must be enabled for the list to take effect. The artefacts are writes to those two registry values, the same module appearing in image load telemetry for unrelated processes, and a module path outside the system directory. The mechanism is switched off when Secure Boot is enabled on Windows 8 and later, so its presence on a modern hardened host is more suspicious than on an old one; legitimate use is rare and normally belongs to security or compatibility software.

beginner.definition: This technique adds an attacker's library to a registry value named AppInit_DLLs. Windows reads that value and loads the library into programs that use another library called user32. Almost every program with a window uses user32, so the attacker's code runs in a great many places. This sub-technique differs from its siblings because user32, and not a process creation call, does the loading.
beginner.whyItMatters: This one value reaches nearly every program on the desktop, so the attacker's code is loaded far more often than with many other persistence tricks. Some of those programs run with higher rights, which can also lift the attacker's access level. Because the change lives only in the registry, a file scan of the system folder may find nothing. Ignoring it leaves a quiet entry point that survives restarts and cleanup attempts.
howItWorks: Windows reads a registry value named AppInit_DLLs in the Windows NT key.
The user32 library reads that list and loads each named library into programs that use it.
Almost every desktop program uses user32, so the list reaches a very large number of processes.
A second value, named LoadAppInit_DLLs, must be switched on for the list to work.
An attacker adds their library path to the value, and administrator rights are needed for that write.
From Windows 8 onward, Secure Boot turns this loading path off, so a modern hardened host rarely uses it.
beginner.example: Think of a large office building with one front desk. Every visitor must pass that desk, and the desk keeps a note that says also admit this extra person with every guest. One note, hundreds of visitors, and nobody checks the name twice. The AppInit value works the same way. One registry entry makes every program that uses user32 carry the attacker's library along with it.
takeaways: AppInit libraries are loaded by user32 into almost every graphical program.
The list needs administrator rights to change, and Secure Boot disables it on newer systems.
An unsigned library loaded by many unrelated programs is a strong warning sign.

objectives: Explain the role of user32 in this technique.
Describe how one registry value can reach so many processes.
Identify the registry values that must be set for the mechanism to work.
Explain why Secure Boot changes the risk on modern Windows.
Detect an unsigned library loaded into many unrelated processes.
Compare AppInit libraries with AppCert libraries and with the parent technique.
